He followed the teaching of the apostles and my teaching in all things, and he lit the Church with his own. The precious stones show this. The great stone on his chest shows the right purpose that he had in defending and explaining the faith. Other stones stand for the many books that he wrote. In glory Thomas is equal to me. His crown of virginity is above mine, but I am above him in the rank of a bishop.”

After this Albert forbade the two friars to tell anyone while he lived, unless an inquiry into the miracles of Saint Thomas and his canonization took place.

Status: told under oath in 1319 by Brother Antony of Brescia, a Dominican priest at Naples. He heard it in Albert’s cell about nine years earlier, in January. Antony’s companion Brother Lanino of Brescia was with him and has since died. Gui tells it too and says that a sworn friar gave the account before the judges.

Source: Naples canonization process, 1319, no. 66, pp. 355–357, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, ch. 51, pp. 215–216, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A monk’s vision of Saint Augustine and Saint Thomas

Dom Gratia of Brescia was a Benedictine monk, a man of great holiness and learning. He followed the teaching of Saint Thomas. Brother Antony of Brescia once spoke of Saint Thomas to him. Dom Gratia said: “My son, I saw, and God revealed to me, that blessed Augustine and Brother Thomas walk under the same yoke in the glory of paradise. I know that holy Brother Thomas was of the greatest purity.”

Status: told under oath in 1319 by Brother Antony of Brescia. He heard it in Dom Gratia’s room near the church of Saint Clement at Brescia. It was about ten years earlier, on the feast of Saint Cecilia.

Source: Naples canonization process, 1319, no. 67, p. 358, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr.

Saint Thomas appears to a royal official in danger

Bartholomew of Capua was a high official of the kingdom of Sicily. Once he suffered a serious persecution. He asked Saint Thomas with devotion to stand beside him and free him from the men who pursued him. One day Saint Thomas appeared to him in visible form. He wore the robe in which Bartholomew used to see him. He said: “Do not fear, for you will be freed, and your enemies will not prevail against you.” Bartholomew did not clearly remember the exact words. He remembered well that he was freed from the persecution in the way Saint Thomas had said, or nearly so.

Bartholomew swore that in all his needs he called on Saint Thomas. He always found the saint kind to him, according to his faith and devotion.

Status: told under oath in 1319 by Bartholomew of Capua, about himself. Gui tells it of a nobleman devoted to Saint Thomas and does not name him.

Source: Naples canonization process, 1319, no. 84, pp. 385–386, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 23, pp. 230–231, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

An official finds a lost saying in the Summa

Bartholomew of Capua had read the writings of Saint Thomas for some years. One day he remembered that he had read there that the custom of the Christian people must be kept as law. He needed those words. He searched for them for many days and could not find them. At last he knelt and asked Saint Thomas to show him where they were. He opened the volume of the Summa called the Second Part of the Second Part. Without turning the pages he found the very words, in the treatise on fasting.

Status: told under oath in 1319 by Bartholomew of Capua, about himself.

Source: Naples canonization process, 1319, no. 84, p. 386, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr.

A thumb of Saint Thomas looks fresh at Anagni

Brother John of Buiano was a Dominican priest and prior of Durazzo. About fifteen years after Saint Thomas died, he came to the provincial chapter at Anagni. There he saw Brother Reginald of Piperno, who had been Saint Thomas’s constant companion. Reginald gave Brother Hugh the thumb of one of Saint Thomas’s hands. Hugh later became bishop of Ostia. The hand had come to Saint Thomas’s sister, the Countess.

The thumb was whole and sound. It looked fresh, like the thumb of a living man. It still had its skin, nail, flesh, bone, and color.

Status: told under oath in 1319 by John of Buiano, who saw the thumb himself. Tocco says that the hand stayed whole except for the thumb, which a devout person took away.

Source: Naples canonization process, 1319, no. 89, pp. 393–394, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also William of Tocco, Ystoria sancti Thome de Aquino, p. 144, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A man thrown from a horse is freed overnight

Peter Boccasicus of Piperno rode a young horse that belonged to the notary Peter Letus. He was going to the town of Sezze to ask the governor to be godfather to Peter Letus’s newborn son. As he came near the governor’s palace, the horse took fright and threw him to the ground. His face and both sides were badly hurt, and he could not get up without help.

Men carried him to the governor’s house. After some treatment from the town’s doctors he mounted again and rode home that day. At home the pain grew worse. He lay in bed through a sleepless night, the next day, and part of the next night.

Then he vowed himself to Saint Thomas of Aquino. He asked the saint to free him from the pain through his mercy, and he promised a silver offering for the tomb and a sung Mass there. He fell asleep. After a little while he woke and called his wife: “Stephania, through the merits of blessed Thomas of Aquino, to whom I commended myself, I am freed by God’s grace. I feel no pain.” On the morning of his oath he came to the tomb and kept his vow.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Peter Boccasicus himself and by his wife Stephania. The fall was on Friday 30 October, and he was freed in the night as Sunday began. Peter Letus swore that he saw Peter Boccasicus well on the Sunday or the Monday. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 6, pp. 417–418; no. 12, p. 424; no. 79, p. 475, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 29, p. 233, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A lay brother’s swollen hands are healed

While he was still a layman, Nicholas Zappus of Piperno had arthritis in both hands for more than a year. His hands were nearly useless, and they hurt. Then he entered the religious life and became a lay brother of Fossanova. About a month later he felt devotion to Saint Thomas of Aquino and commended himself to him. He humbly asked to be freed from the sickness and the pain.

At once he went to the tomb and knelt. He laid his hands on it and held them there for as long as it takes to say the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God” three times. Then he rose, healed and free of pain. It was Easter Sunday. He said that by God’s grace he was healed completely and never felt the sickness again. He told his sisters Gemma and Joan first, and then many others who had seen him sick.

The inquisitors wanted to see if his hands were strong. They told him to lift a weight of a hundred pounds or more. He lifted it easily in front of them and showed them his hands, sound and without swelling.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Nicholas himself. Brother Manuel and Brother Stephen Gozus swore that they had seen him sick and then well. His sister Gemma swore that he told her so. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 7, pp. 418–419; nos. 8 and 13, pp. 420 and 424–425; no. 82, p. 477, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 30, p. 233, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A boy falls from a high loft unhurt

Three boys were learning the shoemaker’s trade at Fossanova under a lay brother named John Maria. John sent them to an upper gallery to beat the dust from his bed cover. One of them was Bartholomew, who was fourteen. He leaned on a board that was not well nailed. It gave way, and he fell with it.

Before he reached the ground he cried out: “Blessed Thomas of Aquino, help me.” He landed on his feet and felt only a little pain. His friend Peter Schimane was thirteen. Peter told him to go to the tomb of Saint Thomas. Bartholomew went there, knelt, and gave thanks. Then he rose without any pain. On the way back Peter asked if he wanted to race. Bartholomew ran with him and ran ahead of him.

The fall was more than the height of three men. The inquisitors and their notaries went to the place and saw it for themselves. It happened fifteen days after Easter in 1320.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by both boys, Bartholomew Leonardi Leonis and Peter Schimane. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, nos. 14–15, pp. 425–427, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 34, pp. 234–235, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A huge swelling is gone before the surgeon cuts

Jacoba Valdebruni of Sonnino had a swelling on one side of her throat as large as two fists. She could hardly breathe, and people could hardly understand her speech. In October 1321 she set out for Piperno to see the surgeon Andrew Papaleo. On the road she heard the bells of the monastery of Fossanova. She thought of Saint Thomas of Aquino, who rests there, and she vowed herself to him with devotion. She asked to be healed without any cutting.

At Piperno the surgeon looked at the swelling and decided to open it with an iron the next day. The next day she had little or no swelling. The surgeon saw that she was almost healed and did not want to touch her with iron. She went home to Sonnino that day. She showed herself to Father James, her parish priest. A small swelling was left, and her voice was clear. A few days later the swelling was gone.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by the priest James Bartholomei of Sonnino, who is her relative. He swore to what he saw and to what she told him. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 17, pp. 428–429, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 36, p. 235, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A girl who twists like a snake is freed

In autumn 1321 a violent pain seized Maria, the seven-year-old daughter of Landulph and Sophia of Sonnino. On a Thursday evening she began to twist like a serpent. Her parents bathed her in warm water, but it did not help. On Friday her mother carried her to the church of Saint Angelo and asked the priest James to read the Gospel of John over her. He read it and sprinkled her with holy water. She was not freed.

The pain went on until Saturday after Vespers. Then Sophia’s mother Julianessa said: “My daughter, commend her to blessed Thomas of Aquino, and she will be freed.” Sophia joined her hands at once and commended the girl to Saint Thomas. She promised that after the healing she would take her to his tomb and offer a wax candle and a gift. At once the girl began to improve. She slept that night, and on Sunday morning she got up fully well. She went outside the town to play with other girls.

Sophia told Father James later: “Blessed be God and blessed Thomas of Aquino. Look, here is my daughter. I vowed her to him. You saw her sick. She is healed by his merits.” The inquisitors and notaries saw that the girl was well that day, because she came with her mother. Her grandmother Julianessa said that it seemed to her as if the girl had died and been raised.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by her mother Sophia, her grandmother Julianessa, and Father James. Gui tells it twice. In his telling she cries out as if she were possessed by a demon.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 18, pp. 429–430; nos. 42–43, pp. 448–450, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, nos. 37 and 93, pp. 235–236 and 252, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A farmer’s burning eyes are healed overnight

Bartholomew Bonihominis of Sonnino was over sixty. In June 1321 a sickness struck his eyes with such burning that it felt as if he had fire in them. He saw little and could not work in the field. He could hardly walk unless he had a stick or a guide. His eyes were so red that others found them hard to look at. The sickness lasted until the middle of October.

On a Tuesday in October around Vespers he humbly commended himself to God and to Saint Thomas of Aquino. He asked Saint Thomas to free him from the pain and the burning and to give back his sight. If the saint did so, he would visit the tomb barefoot with a lighted candle and an offering. No one was there but God and Saint Thomas. The next morning he found himself fully freed. He believed firmly that Saint Thomas had done it.

The inquisitors and notaries examined him. They saw that his eyes were clear and fine and that he saw well.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Bartholomew himself. The priest James of Sonnino, John Varalus, Nicholas Sice, Valdebrunus Leonis, and Floria Nicolai also swore to what they saw and heard. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 30, pp. 438–439; nos. 19–20, pp. 430–431; nos. 23 and 25, pp. 433–435; no. 33, p. 441, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 38, p. 236, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A doctor confirms a groin swelling is gone

For six years and more Amatus Bruni of Sonnino had a swelling in his right groin. It began as large as a hazelnut and grew to the size of an egg. It came from the intestines slipping down. Master Andrew of Julgiano was skilled in such cases, and he advised a truss. A truss is a band that holds such a swelling in. Amatus wore one. The medicines he tried gave no help.

Then he commended himself to Saint Thomas of Aquino. He promised to offer a silver truss at his tomb if he were freed. Within fifteen days he felt completely healed, and he stopped wearing the truss. He said that he had never felt better, even before the sickness began.

The inquisitors ordered their notaries to look at the place. Master Nicholas of Tivoli was there too. He was a doctor in the household of Pandulph of Sabello, one of the inquisitors. They saw no swelling, and Amatus wore no truss. The doctor said that he was healed.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Amatus himself, by his wife Romana, and by his brother Nicholas Bruni. Romana says that she saw and felt the swelling. Amatus himself says it grew to the size of a hen, and his brother says it was the size of an egg or more. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 21, pp. 431–432; no. 24, p. 434; no. 110, pp. 494–495, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 39, p. 236, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A feverish boy of three is found playing

Leo was a boy of about three. In May 1320 he had a fever so hot that on the eighth day his grandmother Floria Nicolai of Sonnino thought he was dead. He lay in bed like a dead child. She vowed the boy to God and to Saint Thomas of Aquino and asked the saint to free him. Then she went to the church of Saint Angelo to hear Mass. She left the boy in his bed.

When she came back from Mass she found him healed. He was walking and playing with his brothers and cousins. That evening his father Crescentius came home from the field. Floria told him: “My son, blessed be God! Your child is healed by the merits of blessed Thomas of Aquino, to whom I commended him.” Crescentius had gone to work on the eighth day, thinking that the boy would die. He marveled when he found him well. On the day of the oath he brought the boy before the inquisitors, healthy and cheerful.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by the grandmother Floria and the father Crescentius Novellus. Gui tells it too and says that the grandmother made the vow.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 22, p. 433; no. 44, p. 450, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 40, p. 236, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A farmer’s cut toe and legs are healed

Bartholomew Theobaldi of Sonnino swore that he had received two cures. People called him Capo Grizo. More than five years before, he was digging with a hoe on a mountain. It was winter, and snow lay on the ground. He struck the big toe of his right foot with the hoe, and it bled. Many surgeons treated him, but nothing helped. One evening, a year or more before his oath, he humbly commended himself to Saint Thomas of Aquino. In the morning he rose healed. Hardly anyone could tell where the wound had been.

He had also suffered for about fifteen years in his shins and feet. He could not walk well, and he hid it. The medicines of Master Andrew Papaleo did not help. A year or more before his oath, he lay in bed and asked Saint Thomas to free him. In the morning he found himself healed and as strong as before. Scars remained on his shins. The inquisitors wanted to see them. They saw the scars and made him walk and run.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Bartholomew himself. Nicholas Barolus swore that he had seen him sick in the legs and then walking well, and that Bartholomew told him why. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, nos. 26–27, pp. 435–436; no. 45, p. 451, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 41, pp. 236–237, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A useless hand is healed on the tomb

In June 1319 Nicholas Infancelli of Sonnino got an abscess in his left hand, between the hand and the arm. For almost a year the hand was useless. Doctors healed the abscess, but they could not give him the use of his hand again.

The next June his mother Adinnaria and he commended themselves to Saint Thomas of Aquino. They asked him to heal the hand so that Nicholas could do farm work. She promised to send him to the tomb at Fossanova. A few days later he came to the tomb. He lay down on it and humbly commended himself again, and he fell asleep there. He woke healed, with full use of his hand. A scar remained. He went home and told his mother, his father, and his sister, and he now works with that hand like any healthy man.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Nicholas himself, by his father Infancellus, and by his sister Saracena. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 28, pp. 436–437; nos. 31–32, pp. 439–441, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 42, p. 237, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A farrier who needed two sticks walks and runs

Master James of Piperno was a farrier and an oblate of Fossanova. He was about sixty years old. In 1321 he had such weakness and pain in his shins and knees that he could not walk without two sticks. This lasted seven weeks. Medicines did him no good, and he had almost lost hope.

One day in August the monks had left the church after Mass, and James went alone to the tomb of Saint Thomas. With humility, devotion, and tears he commended himself to the saint. He took the silk cloth that lay on the tomb and touched his shins and knees with it. He wrapped them in it. At once he rose healed, and from then on he walked without sticks as he had before the sickness.

As he left the church he saw Brother Nicholas of Frusinone, the prior, in front of it. He said: “Write down that God has freed me through the merits of blessed Thomas of Aquino, as you see.” The inquisitors and notaries saw him walking and running freely.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by James himself. Brother Nicholas of Frusinone, Brother Leonard Sacurella, and John Cossa swore that they saw him sick and then well. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, nos. 38–41, pp. 444–448, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 44, p. 237, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A carpenter brother’s arm is healed overnight

Brother Valdebrunus was a lay brother and the carpenter of Fossanova. He was about forty, and he had been in the monastery for thirty-seven years. Around Christmas 1319 a pain seized his right arm and shoulder one night in bed. From then until the feast of Saint Andrew he could not use the arm or the hand. He could not do his carpenter’s work, and he could not sleep on his right side. He was put in the infirmary with the other sick.

One night he devoutly and humbly commended himself to Saint Thomas of Aquino. He promised a silver offering for the tomb if Saint Thomas freed him. He fell asleep. In the morning he got up completely healed.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Valdebrunus himself and by Peter Amati, an oblate of the monastery. Peter says that he saw him sick for almost a year and then at his work again. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 29, pp. 437–438; no. 112, pp. 495–496, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 43, p. 237, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A tailor’s finger is healed twice

Nicholas of Aprutio was a tailor in Terracina. One evening in June or July 1320, the first finger of his right hand became painful, swollen, and black. He often had arthritis in his feet, and now he had it in his left hand too. He feared that he would lose the work of cutting and sewing cloth, and so his living.

That night he commended himself to Saint Thomas of Aquino with tears, and his wife Formosa heard him. He asked the saint to free the finger of his right hand, so that he would not be useless. For his left hand and his feet he asked nothing. He promised to bring a silver hand to the tomb. Then he went to bed and slept. He woke and said: “Formosa, I do not feel pain in my finger. Go, light the lamp so that we can see.” In the light the finger had no swelling or blackness, and its color was as before.

The second event came in November 1321. The inquisitors had called him to testify, and on the Sunday he wanted to set out. His feet hurt, so he sent his wife to the monastery to ask for a later day. As soon as she left, the pain came back to his finger. He feared the saint’s anger and decided to go. He asked for the help of Saint Thomas, so that he could come in spite of his feet and the finger would stop hurting. At once the finger stopped hurting, and his feet were better. He walked and rode, and he reached the inquisitors the same day.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Nicholas and by his wife Formosa. The inquisitors and notaries saw him walking well and his finger sound on the day of his oath. Gui tells the second event.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, nos. 54–57, pp. 457–460, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 48, pp. 238–239, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A trembling man sees a Dominican in a dream

Bartholomew Bennicasse of Sermoneta was about fifty. For more than four years he had trembled in his legs and hands. In August 1320 a fever came too, and it troubled him on and off until May 1321. He hid the trembling as well as he could. One day in May he devoutly commended himself to Saint Thomas of Aquino. He asked to be freed from the trembling and the fever.

That night, as he fell asleep, he saw a tall and handsome man in the robe of a Dominican. Bartholomew firmly believed that it was Saint Thomas. The friar touched him on the chest and on his limbs. At once Bartholomew woke and called his wife Bona: “Bona, I am freed. I vowed myself to blessed Thomas of Aquino, and he was with me and freed me.” He found himself healed of the fever, the trembling, and the pains, and he never felt them again.

Leonard Palumbus was a notary of Sermoneta. He had often told Bartholomew to drink less wine. Bartholomew met him at harvest time and told him that he was freed through the merits of Saint Thomas of Aquino. He said it “to your shame.” Leonard says that Bartholomew then drank even more than before.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Bartholomew and by his wife Bona. The notary Leonard Palumbus swore that he saw the trembling and the cure. The inquisitors and notaries saw Bartholomew sound. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, nos. 58–60, pp. 460–462, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 49, p. 239, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A man sick in his liver is healed

Peter Craparius of Sermoneta was sick from the week of Easter until June 1321. He had a sickness of the liver. His skin was as yellow as saffron, he had no appetite, and his limbs felt heavy. One day he lay weak in his garden by the gate of Sermoneta. He heard Bartholomew Bennicasse tell others at the gate how he had been cured of his trembling through Saint Thomas of Aquino.

Peter felt devotion, and he commended himself to Saint Thomas at the hour of Vespers. That evening after Vespers he was getting ready for bed when he felt healed. The next morning he told his wife Marotta and his son Peter. From then on he was well.

Master John Rubeus was a doctor of Sermoneta. He swore that he had seen Peter’s urine with all the signs of the sickness. He advised bloodletting. Six or eight days later he saw Peter fully healed. He wondered at it, because by the art of medicine Peter should not have recovered so quickly.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Peter Craparius himself, by his wife Marotta, by their son Peter, and by the doctor John Rubeus. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, nos. 61–64, pp. 462–465, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 50, p. 239, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A three-year-old boy is freed from the falling sickness

Guido was a son of Master John of Piperno. He brought his little son Stephen before the inquisitors. The boy was three years old. For more than a year and a half he had had the falling sickness, which is called epilepsy. It struck him once or twice at each change of the moon. Sometimes it struck him three, four, or even six times.

Guido feared that his son would die. He devoutly commended him to Saint Thomas of Aquino. Then he carried him to the tomb and laid him on it. From then on the boy was freed, and he never felt the sickness again.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by the father Guido. The boy’s uncles Andrew Francisci and Master Nicholas, a doctor, also swore to what they had seen. So did the surgeon Gregory of Julgiano and a neighbor, Lady Maria Barrola. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 72, p. 469; no. 91, pp. 483–484; no. 97, pp. 486–487; no. 106, p. 492; no. 130, pp. 507–508, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 53, p. 240, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A sick baby is healed after his mother’s vow

Gemma Gregorii of Piperno was over sixty years old. Her son James Salatinus was now thirty-six or more. In his first year of life he had such a sickness that the ribs at the front seemed joined to his loins. He could hardly breathe out. Gemma, many other women, and the doctors who saw him thought he would die.

A neighbor named Lady Stephania Sebastiana urged Gemma to turn to Saint Thomas. Gemma knelt and commended the child to Saint Thomas of Aquino. She promised to send him to the tomb with an offering. At once the child improved and was healed, and he is still alive.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Gemma, the boy’s mother. She says that the others who saw it have died. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 73, p. 470, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 54, p. 240, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A fever ends after a dream of Saint Thomas

Matthew of Noria of Piperno was about fifty. From August 1321 he had quartan fever, which came back every fourth day. He could eat nothing but apples and sorb apples. Each attack held him from morning until evening. On Friday 30 October he stood in front of his house, angry at his sickness. His neighbor Peter Letus said to him: “Do not torment yourself. Go back into your house and rest. Commend yourself to blessed Thomas of Aquino, that he may free you.”

Matthew went in. He commended himself to the Blessed Virgin Mary of Rippa, whose church stands near Piperno. Matthew also commended himself to Saint Thomas, who lies at Fossanova. If he were freed, he would go on his knees from the door of the church of Fossanova to the tomb. He would also bind the tomb with a silver thread. After the vow he fell asleep.

In his sleep he stood near the church of Saint Mary of Rippa. He saw a friar in the robe of a Dominican coming along the road from Fossanova to that church. The friar had a staff in his hand. When the friar reached the church, the Virgin came out and said: “Thomas, where are you going?” The friar answered: “I am going to help a poor man who does not stop calling on me.” Then it seemed to Matthew that Saint Thomas came to him and uncovered him.

Matthew woke at once and got out of bed. He called his wife Bellitia: “Bellitia, the quartan fever will never seize me again, because blessed Thomas of Aquino has uncovered me. So I believe that I am healed.” He never had the fever again. He said that by God’s grace, through the merits of Saint Thomas, he was well and able to do what healthy men do.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Matthew himself, by his wife Bellitia, and by Peter Letus. Peter swore that Matthew told him the next day that Saint Thomas had appeared to him in the night and freed him. Gui tells it too and calls him Matthew of Voria.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, nos. 75–76, pp. 471–473; no. 80, p. 476, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 56, p. 241, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A boy is healed without surgery after a prayer

John Garini of Piperno was a boy of nearly eight. He was born with the right testicle larger than the left, and it grew day by day to the size of a hen’s egg. It was as hard as wood, and the intestine slipped down into the pouch. He wore a truss. The doctors were Master Gregory and Master Leonard of Julgiano. They said that it could not be healed without cutting. They added that if they cut him, they would expect him to die. His grandfather John grieved and would not give him to the doctors.

His grandmother Maria Simeonis heard of the fame of Saint Thomas of Aquino. She believed that the boy could be healed without cutting, and that a child’s prayer might be heard sooner. She taught him to say: “Dear blessed Thomas of Aquino, if you will heal me of my sickness without any cutting, I will come to your tomb. I will bring a silver offering in the shape of my own figure, when you are canonized.” As he said these words in her presence, he began to improve. Soon he was fully healed.

About eight months after his healing, his family brought him before the inquisitors. The inquisitors and notaries saw him healed.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by the grandmother Maria Simeonis, the grandfather John Garini, the father Peter, and the doctors Gregory and Leonard of Julgiano. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, nos. 77–78, pp. 473–475; no. 89, pp. 482–483; no. 92, p. 484; no. 94, p. 485, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 57, p. 241, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

Two women of Piperno are freed from arm pain

Schimana was a woman of Piperno, over fifty years old. For about four years she had pain in her right shoulder, arm, and finger. She could not spin. On the feast of Saint Martin in 1321 she came to Fossanova. That was eight days before she gave her oath. She devoutly vowed herself to Saint Thomas of Aquino. She promised a silver offering worth twelve pence if he freed her. From then on she felt no pain.

Lady Lea Pennazola came with her. Lea had the same pain in her right shoulder and arm, and Schimana swore that she was freed too. Lea told a longer story herself. For a year and a half she could not use that arm. One day she heard that relics of Saint Thomas had been brought to the church of Saint Mary at Piperno. She went there and saw the relics on the high altar. She commended herself to Saint Thomas and laid her arm on the case that was said to hold them. At once she was healed, and she used the arm as before. This was on a Sunday in May 1320.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Schimana and by Lea herself. Lea’s daughter-in-law Romica swore that she saw Lea sick and then well. Gui tells both accounts.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 83, p. 478; nos. 99 and 101–103, pp. 488–490, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, nos. 59 and 66, pp. 242 and 244, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A man’s fever and vomiting stop at once

Peter Ectari of Piperno was at Mass in the church of Saint Mary on a Sunday in October 1321, the Sunday before the feast of Saint Luke. A strong fever seized him. He went home, and the fever and vomiting afflicted him so badly that he feared he would die. His wife Gayta urged him to commend himself to Saint Thomas of Aquino. He did so that same day, and she heard him. His mother and a friend were also in the room. At once the fever and the vomiting stopped.

He was so well that on the Tuesday he set out on a trip. He says that he went to Calabria. His wife and his aunt say that he went to a fair in the kingdom within three days.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Peter himself, by his wife Gayta, and by his aunt Maria Pepe. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 121, pp. 501–502; no. 132, pp. 508–509; no. 133, p. 509, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 74, p. 246, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A lay brother in Sicily regains his speech

Brother Peter Crescentii of Piperno was a lay brother of Fossanova. About three years before his oath he was in Sicily, at the monastery’s farm of Saint Christopher. One morning a swelling came on his face and throat. He could not speak. He could not open his mouth, even when a man tried to open it with a knife.

A man of Piperno named Nicholas of Monte San Giovanni was there. He advised Peter to commend himself to Saint Thomas of Aquino. Peter could not speak, so he commended himself humbly in his heart. Nicholas saw him join his hands. At about the ninth hour Peter fell asleep. At the hour of Vespers he woke healthy and able to speak, and the swelling had mostly gone down. Nicholas heard him begin to speak and confess his sins to Brother Gregory of Cisterna, a monk who was there. The swelling later left him completely.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Peter himself and by Nicholas of Monte San Giovanni, who was with him. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 85, pp. 479–480; no. 104, pp. 490–491, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 61, pp. 242–243, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A deaf man hears even low voices

Nicholas Picardi of Terracina had a ringing in his ears and was nearly deaf for fifteen days. He could hardly hear people who spoke to him, even in a loud voice. He came to Piperno and thought about the miracles that God worked through Saint Thomas of Aquino. At the midday meal on the day before his oath he commended himself to Saint Thomas. His friends Nicholas Taurellus and James Cafassus were with him.

The next morning he got up and heard well. The inquisitors and notaries saw that he heard well, even words spoken in a low voice. His friend James Cafassus swore that during the fifteen days Nicholas had said to him and to others: “I do not hear you.” Both friends swore that they saw him hear well the next morning.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Nicholas Picardi and by his two friends. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, nos. 86–88, pp. 480–482, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 62, p. 243, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A wife who lost her speech is healed

Jacoba was the wife of Nicholas Petri Nicholai of Piperno. In November 1321 she had a continuous fever for five days. It made her so weak that she lost her speech. On the fifth day people thought that she was dying. Her mother-in-law Herminia Luce, her husband, and others stood around her and wept.

Her husband commended her to Saint Thomas of Aquino. He promised to bring a lamp, a candle, and money for a Mass to the tomb if Saint Thomas healed her. At once she began to vomit. Her speech came back, the fever left her, and she was healed. Her husband kept his vow.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by her husband Nicholas. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 111, p. 495, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 68, p. 244, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A man crying that he is dying is freed

On Sunday 8 November 1321 after Vespers a great pain struck Peter Carolus of Terracina in his head and his whole body. He cried out until bedtime, and he believed that he would soon die. The women in the room believed it too. His wife and his daughter called Lady Gemma Ronilgione and Mabilia, the sister of Raynald Bulizola, to come.

Both women said to him: “Peter, commend yourself to blessed Thomas of Aquino.” He commended himself at once with devotion. While the women still stood there, he vomited heavily and was freed from all the pain. Mabilia says that he said to her: “Dear Mabilia, blessed be God and blessed Thomas of Aquino, through whose merits I am freed.”

A boy named Leonard Bulizola swore that he came to the house and heard Peter cry out: “I am dying, I am dying! Let the priest come!” Leonard was about thirteen. He saw Peter freed.

Status: told under oath in 1321, eight days later. Peter himself swore to it, and so did Gemma, Mabilia, and the boy Leonard.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, nos. 49–53, pp. 453–457, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr.

A child with a flow of blood is healed

Julianessa of Sonnino had a little grandson named Nicholutius, the son of her son Peter. For almost a year he had a flow of blood, and she firmly believed that he would die. When Brother William of Tocco came to Sonnino, she said to him: “Brother William, if blessed Thomas gave us this boy back, it would be a great miracle.”

Tocco said: “Bring him to me at the church of Saint Angelo in this town, and we will commend him to blessed Thomas of Aquino.” She carried the boy to the church. There she and Tocco commended him to Saint Thomas. At once the boy began to improve. Within a few days he was fully well, and the flow of blood stopped. As far as she knows, he has had no illness since.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Julianessa. A year had passed since the cure, and the boy was then six. She names her husband Bertraymus Varolus, her son Peter, her daughter-in-law Alcruda, and Tocco as people who knew of it.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 46, pp. 451–452, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr.

A young man carries a lance to the tomb

Nicolucius Affinnati of Piperno was about twenty. For three months he had a pain in his right shoulder and arm, and he could not lift the arm to his mouth. On a Saturday in September 1320 he commended himself to Saint Thomas of Aquino and asked to be freed. His wife Leonarda was with him. On Sunday morning he got up and found himself healed. That same morning he came to the tomb and offered a candle, as he had vowed.

His brothers Frederick and Barbatus walked with him. Barbatus was sixteen. He swore that Nicolucius carried a lance in the hand of his bad arm. At first he did not seem to carry it freely. After they had visited the tomb, Barbatus saw him carry the lance well. From then on he did everything as a healthy man does.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Nicolucius and by his brother Barbatus. Gui tells it too.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 118, pp. 499–500; no. 127, pp. 505–506, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 72, p. 245, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A cleric’s bloody cough ends at the tomb

Master Marcus was a cleric of the church of Saint Lucy at Piperno. Sixteen years before his oath he began to have a cough that lasted three years. Each winter, from its start until about May, he coughed hard and spat thick phlegm. Blood poured from his mouth and nose, two or three times a day.

One day in March he came to Fossanova. He humbly commended himself to Saint Thomas of Aquino and laid himself on the tomb. Lady Guerra Gulferama of Piperno and Dom Peter Andreae, a monk, were present. Marcus went back to Piperno. That night he vomited a large amount of blood, and from then on he was well. This was thirteen years before his oath, in the week of the Annunciation.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Master Marcus himself. Gui tells it too. Tocco’s list tells a similar account of a man named Marcus Brachialis of Piperno.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, no. 124, pp. 503–504, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr. Also Bernard Gui, Vita S. Thomae, no. 75, p. 246 and William of Tocco, Ystoria sancti Thome de Aquino, catalogue no. 27, p. 153, in Prümmer, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 1, https://archive.org/details/prummerfontesvitaestho.

A woman’s quartan fever ends after she prays twice

In October 1321 Lady Gemma Ronilgione of Terracina had six attacks of quartan fever. Fourteen years before she had had it for a year and a half, and it had made her so weak that she thought she would die. She feared that this fever would last as long. Humbly and devoutly she commended herself to Saint Thomas of Aquino and asked him to take the fever away. She had one more attack after that prayer. Then she commended herself again and said that she would tell everyone if he freed her. After that she had no more attacks.

She says that she has told it to more than a thousand people. Her son Ceccus swore that he heard her pray at the hour of the attack: “Blessed Thomas, you allow me to have the quartan fever again. Free me through the mercy of God.” She was also the woman who told Peter Carolus to commend himself to Saint Thomas, “who healed me before.”

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Gemma and by her son Ceccus Ronilgione.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, nos. 50–51, pp. 454–456; no. 105, p. 491, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr.

A monk leads his sick kinsman to the tomb

Peter Nicholai of Sonnino had weak and swollen legs and feet for a year. He could hardly walk. One day he came to Fossanova in great pain to see his kinsman Brother Leo of Sonnino. Leo was a monk there. Peter complained of his weakness. Leo said: “Let us go to the tomb of blessed Thomas of Aquino, and commend yourself to him.”

They went. Peter knelt before the tomb and commended himself to Saint Thomas. He asked the saint to free him from the sickness. Then he lay down near the tomb. In that hour he felt better, and within four days he was completely healed. The swelling left his feet and legs, and he was as strong as before. This was about fourteen months before his oath.

Status: told under oath in 1321 by Peter himself and by his neighbor Bartholomew Mezettus. Brother Leo led him to the tomb. When Peter swore his oath, he said that Leo was in Sicily.

Source: Fossanova canonization process, 1321, nos. 47–48, pp. 452–453, in Laurent, Fontes vitae S. Thomae Aquinatis, fasc. 4, https://archive.org/details/fontesvitaesthom00pr.

Bernard Gui ended his list with these words: “God has worked many other miracles through the merits of Thomas Aquinas in different parts of the world. They are not written in this book.”

A note on the sources. The bull and the sworn witnesses of 1319 and 1321 are the Church’s formal record. Most of the healings on this page come from those witnesses. Most of the visions and wonders of Saint Thomas’s own life come from the early Lives, written between about 1300 and 1323. Some stories are told in more than one way, and this page gives each telling with the name of its teller. The early Lives and the canonization documents read for this page do not give the saying about miracles and articles.

teachings.teachings:
Thomas Aquinas wrote theology for teaching: the Summa contra Gentiles, the Summa Theologiae (still unfinished when he stopped writing in December 1273), commentaries on Scripture and on Aristotle, and disputed questions. Some of his sermons survive only as listeners took them down. The themes below give his own words, with the work and place, and a fact from his life that shows how he lived what he taught. Translations are our own unless a public-domain translator is named.

Faith and reason

Thomas held that our salvation needed a teaching revealed by God, besides the philosophy that human reason works out. Theology uses philosophy and the other sciences as handmaids, he wrote, because of the weakness of our minds and through no lack of its own. He put the principle in one sentence near the start of the Summa Theologiae.

“Since grace does not destroy nature but perfects it, natural reason must serve faith.”

— Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 1, a. 8, ad 2 (our translation)

This is the source of the familiar phrase “grace perfects nature.” He wrote it in the opening question of the Summa, which asks what theology is. He lived it by setting Aristotle and the whole of reason to work for the faith, and on his deathbed he left everything he had said to the correction of the Church.

What we can know of God

Thomas believed that the mind can reason from the world to God, from motion and from the order of nature. His “five ways” begin with what anyone can see, that “some things in this world are moved,” and the fifth ends, “and this we call God.” Yet he insisted that about God we cannot know what he is, only what he is not, and that even a little knowledge of God is worth more than great certainty about small things.

“The least that can be known of the highest things is more to be desired than the most certain knowledge of the smallest things.”

— Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I, q. 1, a. 5, ad 1 (our translation)

In the same reply he compares the human mind before the things of God to an owl’s eye dazzled by the sun. He lived this teaching most plainly in December 1273, when, by one sworn account, he stopped writing and said that all he had written seemed like straw beside what he had seen.

Love, mercy, and friendship with God

To love, Thomas wrote, is to will good to someone. God loves everything that exists, and his love pours out and creates the goodness in things. Mercy belongs to God most of all in what it does; among the virtues that concern our neighbor, mercy is the greatest. Charity, the love that unites us to God, is a kind of friendship.

“Charity is a kind of friendship of man with God.”

— Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 23, a. 1 (our translation)

He added that it would be ridiculous to speak of friendship with wine or with a horse. In his own life the friend we see most clearly is his companion Reginald of Piperno, who heard his secrets and kept them.

Law, justice, and the common good

Thomas defined law as reason’s ordering of a community toward its common good. The first precept of the natural law, which he called the light of understanding placed in us by God, is that good is to be done and pursued, and evil avoided. Justice is the constant and lasting will to give each person what is due. He also wrote that Jews and pagans must in no way be forced to believe, because belief is an act of the will; in the same article he allowed that heretics and apostates might be compelled.

“Law is an ordinance of reason for the common good, made by the one who has care of the community, and promulgated.”

— Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I-II, q. 90, a. 4 (our translation)

The definition comes from his treatise on law in the second part of the Summa. Kings sought his counsel: Louis IX of France asked his advice in hard cases, and Charles of Anjou paid him to teach at Naples.

Handing on what is contemplated

Thomas belonged to the Order of Preachers, and he wrote that it is greater to hand on to others what one has contemplated than only to contemplate. Christ himself, he wrote, chose a life of preaching and teaching, handing on to others what he contemplated.

“As it is greater to illuminate than only to shine, so it is greater to hand on to others what one has contemplated than only to contemplate.”

— Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 188, a. 6 (our translation)

This is the true source of the popular phrase about giving others “the fruits of contemplation.” He lived it in Naples in 1273, where he lectured each day and preached through Lent on the Our Father in his own Neapolitan, to crowds that a witness said were almost the whole city.

Rest and play

Thomas thought rest was a moral matter. The soul’s rest is delight, and a person who never relaxes will break. He retold the story of St. John the Evangelist and the bow that would break if it were always bent, and named a virtue for good humor in play, eutrapelia. Play, he wrote, should be used like sleep and other rest, once serious duties are done.

“The mind of man would break if it were never relaxed from its tension.”

— Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae II-II, q. 168, a. 2 (our translation)

The man who wrote this was known for being so absorbed that a bowl could be set before him and taken away without his noticing; he also left the friars’ garden recreation to be alone.

The Eucharist

By his own deathbed words, Thomas had “taught and written much” on the Eucharist, and, by the witness of Ptolemy of Lucca, he composed the office for the feast of Corpus Christi at the command of Pope Urban IV. Modern scholars judge his authorship of those hymns, and of the prayer Adoro te devote, probable but not certain. Their theme is that the senses fail before the sacrament, and faith alone suffices.

“Sight, touch, and taste are deceived in you, but by hearing alone it is safe to believe.”

— Adoro te devote, ascribed to Thomas Aquinas (our translation)

At Fossanova, receiving Communion for the last time, he professed that the Host was true God and true man, and said that he had studied, kept watch, and worked for love of him, leaving all he had said about the sacrament to the correction of the Roman Church.

The love of wisdom

For Thomas, study was a joy. It belongs to the wise man to set things in order, he wrote, and truth must be the last end of the whole universe. A small error at the start becomes a great one at the end, so the beginning must be right.

“Of all human pursuits, the pursuit of wisdom is the more perfect, the more sublime, the more useful, and the more agreeable.”

— Thomas Aquinas, Summa contra Gentiles I.2, tr. Joseph Rickaby, 1905

He wrote this at the opening of the Summa contra Gentiles. He showed what he meant on a walk near Paris: told that he could sell the whole city to the king, he answered that he would rather have Chrysostom on Matthew.

gaps: Biography: 8,018 words by the lint count (narrative plus the source note and research paragraph), at the low end of tier A; 14 story chapters, 10 block quotes; lint has no MUST FIX lines and 3 CHECK lines for long sentences inside quotations.

Not read: the Fossanova testimonies of 1321, most of Gui’s death chapters, most of the Naples process (only the depositions of Bartholomew of Capua, Peter of Monte San Giovanni, Tocco and a few others were re-read), Pius XI’s Studiorum Ducem, Torrell, Weisheipl, the Sentences commentary, the Quodlibets, Mirabilis Deus (1567), the Acta Sanctorum, Gerard de Frachet’s own text. The Latin bull is printed in the Fontes volume but was not read in full; the English translation was used.

Straw saying: only Bartholomew of Capua’s sworn account (art. 79), which by its own text came to him in 1303 from John del Giudice of Anagni, to whom Reginald had confessed it in his last illness (checked against the Fontes text). In that account the oath and the full words follow the visit to San Severino. Tocco, Calo and Gui give the San Severino version without “straw.”

Dumb ox and talking crucifix: first in Calo, Tocco and Gui (c. 1317–1323); not in the 1319 depositions (checked by search of the Fontes text); told as legend. Tocco gives the nickname as fact and introduces only Albert’s words with “fertur” (it is said).

Conflicts attributed in the text: jailer (Tocco and Gui: mother; Bartholomew: father); escape (Tocco: mother let him down; Ptolemy: Thomas arranged it); herrings (Peter: ate; Tocco and Abbot Nicholas: refused); funeral preacher (Tocco’s life: Reginald; Tocco’s testimony: Peter of Sezze); days from last Communion to death (Tocco: unction next day; Peter: third day).

Unverified: Landulf’s death year (would bear on the jailer question); birth year (c. 1225 from Tocco, 1227 in Calo and Baring-Gould); age at entry (Gui 14, Ptolemy 16); the exact Panis angelicus stanza; the Mirabilis Deus day (11 or 15 April 1567); the 1969 decree date; when the body passed to the Count of Fondi (1304 in Conway, 1348 in Wikipedia). The “What is God?” question is in Calo only.

Wrongly credited or unproven lines kept out of the quotes: “Hominem unius libri timeo” (first credited by Jeremy Taylor, 1649); “To one who has faith, no explanation is necessary” (Werfel film, 1943); “The things that we love tell us what we are” (no locator); De modo studendi (Ignotus Auctor per Corpus Thomisticum); Creator ineffabilis (Corpus Thomisticum: unknown author) and Concede michi (Corpus Thomisticum: authenticity doubtful; only in a late recension of Tocco); “as many miracles as articles” (tradition).

Reported words: the Credo and Ten Commandments sermons are reportationes (Reginald; Peter of Andria) and are marked “as taken down.” The Fossanova viaticum prayer is Tocco’s version; Peter’s sworn version is shorter.

Rights: Corpus Thomisticum digital editions are copyrighted; only a line or two of Latin is quoted, with our own English. Dominican Fathers 1920 and Rickaby 1905 are public domain. The FSSPX bull translation is facts-only; only the short phrase on life and miracles is paraphrased.
